title.en: Powering the Future: Batteries, Grids, and Smart Homes
Where Does the Power Go at Night?

A2.text: At night the sun completely stops shining, and some days the wind stops blowing too. So where does your power come from then? Batteries and smart grids are the answer.

B1.text: At night the sun disappears, and some days the wind barely blows at all. Batteries and smart grids increasingly provide the answer to where our electricity then comes from.

B2.text: Once the sun sets or the wind falls completely still, conventional generation alone cannot keep the lights on. This discussion investigates precisely where that missing power is actually supposed to come from.

title.en: SDG 7's Other Half: Reliable and Modern
title.zh: SDG7的另一半：穩定與現代化

A2.text: SDG 7 is not only about clean power. It is also about power that never stops operating. Today's talk is about keeping the lights on all the time.

B1.text: SDG 7 is not only about clean power generation, but also about power that keeps working reliably whatever the weather. This talk focuses on keeping a grid that depends on the weather running.

B2.text: SDG 7 actually covers more than clean generation alone. It equally demands reliability, meaning power that keeps flowing whatever the weather, so today's focus falls squarely on modern, resilient infrastructure.

title.en: A Grid That Has Already Wobbled

A2.text: Taiwan's whole power grid shook once before. It happened quite badly, really. In 2022, one small switch problem cut power to millions of homes right across the island.

B1.text: Taiwan's power grid has already wobbled once before this. In 2022, a single switch failure triggered a cascade that cut power to millions of households across the island.

B2.text: Although rarely discussed outside engineering circles, Taiwan's power grid has already buckled once before under pressure. A single switch failure back in 2022 cascaded into serious outages across a wide share of the island.

stages.language_pattern: present progressive for trends / this causes ...

title.en: When Weather Becomes the Fuel

A2.text: Clean power now takes up more and more of our grid. Last year wind power jumped a lot, by about 66 percent. So guessing our future power supply is getting harder.

B1.text: Renewable power now makes up a growing share of the grid. Wind generation alone has increased by about 66 percent in just one year, which makes supply much harder to forecast.

B2.text: Renewable generation now dominates the grid's day-to-day swings in output. Wind generation alone has climbed roughly 66 percent in a single year, complicating forecasting far beyond what planners once assumed.

title.en: One Switch, Five Million Homes

A2.text: In 2022, one broken switch in the south caused a chain reaction. Power plants shut down one after another. Almost 5.5 million homes lost power that day.

B1.text: In 2022, one broken switch in the south triggered a chain reaction across three regional grids. Almost 5.5 million households lost power within a short window that day.

B2.text: Back in 2022, a fault in just one switch located in the south rippled outward, cascading across three separate regional grids at once. Within minutes, almost 5.5 million households were left without electricity.

title.en: Chips Draw Power Like Never Before

A2.text: Our chip plants now need much more power every year. One plant alone uses about 9 percent of everything we generate. Our grid is too old for this new demand.

B1.text: Chip factories now draw huge and rising amounts of electricity, and one factory alone uses close to 9 percent of the national total. Our grid was never designed for loads like this.

B2.text: Chip plants now use an enormous and steadily growing share of national power. One firm alone accounts for roughly 9 percent of total demand that older infrastructure was never designed for.

title.en: Taipower Passes One Gigawatt of Storage

A2.text: Taipower has now built a huge amount of battery storage. The Dongshan site started work in November 2024. That storage is real and working today.

B1.text: Taipower has now reached about one full gigawatt of battery storage connected to the grid. One site, at Dongshan, started running in November 2024, clearly showing the idea works at real scale.

B2.text: Battery storage on Taiwan's whole grid has now passed one full gigawatt in total. That milestone came partly from the Dongshan site, which first started running back in November 2024.

title.en: 3.5 Million Meters, Talking Back

A2.text: Smart meters now sit in over 3.5 million homes. They send data back to Taipower all day. That data helps the grid react much faster.

B1.text: Taipower has installed smart meters for over 3.5 million customers, reaching more than 80 percent of all power use. That real-time data is exactly what a smart grid needs.

B2.text: More than 3.5 million customers across Taiwan now have a Taipower smart meter installed, covering upwards of 80 percent of the country's total power consumption. That constant flow of data is exactly what a modern grid depends on.

title.en: From a Niche Market to a Growth Story
title.zh: 從利基市場到成長故事

A2.text: Taiwan's storage market was once quite small. Now it is a growing business worth billions of dollars already. By 2030 it could grow even bigger than today.

B1.text: Taiwan's whole storage market has grown from a tiny niche into a business worth billions of dollars. One forecast expects it to keep expanding sharply all the way through 2030.

B2.text: Taiwan's whole energy-storage sector has expanded from a fairly tiny niche into an industry worth billions of dollars today. One projection expects continued rapid growth all the way through 2030.

title.en: Why Grid Batteries Choose Safety Over Range
title.zh: 電網儲能為何選安全不選續航

A2.text: Grid batteries do not need long range like a car battery. Instead, they need to be safe and last for years. So most now use a different battery type.

B1.text: Instead of the dense chemistry used in electric cars, most new grid batteries now use a chemistry called LFP. This trades away some range for safety and a longer working life.

B2.text: Rather than the energy-dense chemistry used in electric cars, most new grid-scale batteries rely on a chemistry known as LFP. That choice trades away some range for durability, safety and lower cost.

title.en: Software Moves the Power Now
title.zh: 現在是軟體在調度電力

A2.text: This type is called LFP. It is safer and lasts far longer than other types. Most new grid batteries in the world now use it.

B1.text: LFP battery cells last through thousands of charging cycles and rarely ever catch fire. That combination matters more for a fixed grid battery than raw energy density ever could.

B2.text: Built for thousands of charge cycles, LFP cells also resist fire remarkably well. That combination suits stationary grid storage far better than the raw energy density that vehicles prize, while keeping overall costs relatively low.

title.en: Your Rooftop as Part of the Plant
title.zh: 你家屋頂也是電廠的一部分

A2.text: Instead of only building power plants, Taipower now lets software move the power around. Your own roof could join this. So could your battery, or even your car.

B1.text: Instead of only building new power plants, Taipower's smart grid software now routes power in near real time. Rooftop solar, home batteries and even electric cars could soon join that same system.

B2.text: Taipower increasingly prefers software-driven routing over building yet another power plant, shifting electricity across the grid in near real time. Rooftop solar panels, home batteries and electric cars are steadily being absorbed into that very same network.

title.en: More Sensors, More Doors to Guard
title.zh: 更多感測器，更多要顧的門

A2.text: More sensors and more software also mean more doors for hackers. Hackers now have many more ways to try. If one system fails, the whole grid could feel it fast.

B1.text: More sensors and more connected software also create more doors that a hacker could try. If a smart grid's control system is compromised, the damage could spread quickly.

B2.text: A larger set of sensors and connected software creates more entry points for attackers to try. Only when a system's defences are fully secured will that added risk actually diminish over time.

title.en: Who Pays for the Smarter Grid

A2.text: All these new batteries and meters cost real money. Someone has to pay for them. Right now, that cost often lands on our electricity bills.

B1.text: This growing storage industry is good news for Taiwan's tech sector. But someone still has to pay for all these batteries and meters, usually through higher electricity rates.

B2.text: This whole fast-growing storage industry benefits Taiwan's broader technology sector quite considerably. Yet someone still has to bear the cost of every battery and meter, typically through higher electricity tariffs.

title.en: A Two-Speed Grid in the Making?

A2.text: Not every family can pay for a smart meter, a battery, or an electric car right away. Some families will wait longer. Without a plan, that gap will only get bigger.

B1.text: Wealthier households can usually afford smart meters, home batteries and electric cars first. Poorer households may have to wait far longer, and that gap could widen if nobody plans ahead.

B2.text: Wealthier households nowadays tend to gain access to smart meters, home batteries and electric vehicles first. Poorer households may have to wait much longer, widening a gap that policy alone must address.

title.en: Smart Still Has to Mean Fair

A2.text: So these same new tools can actually fix one problem well. But they can also create brand new ones. A smart grid must be safe, fair, and shared by everyone.

B1.text: So the very tools that solve one problem can quietly create new ones. A smart grid must also be genuinely judged on safety, fairness and who actually gets access to it.

B2.text: The very same tools that resolve one technical problem can quietly generate several brand-new ones. A smart grid must therefore be judged on safety and fairness first, not efficiency alone.

title.en: Built in Real Time, Slide by Slide

A2.text: To wrap up, Taiwan's grid is being rebuilt right now. New batteries and sensors now work together every day. This is not only about wires and power plants anymore.

B1.text: To wrap up, engineers are rebuilding Taiwan's grid piece by piece while it keeps running. New batteries, sensors and software now sit right alongside wiring and plants that are already decades old.

B2.text: Piece by piece, and without ever fully switching off, Taiwan's electrical grid is undergoing a quiet transformation. Fresh batteries, sensors and control software now coexist with infrastructure that has, in some cases, served the island for decades.

title.en: This Is Your Design Problem Now

A2.text: This matters directly to you. You are the future engineers in this room. You will design the next battery, the next chip, or the next line of safety code.

B1.text: This whole issue is not abstract for anyone in this room. You represent the next generation of engineers who will shape the batteries, algorithms and safety systems still to come.

B2.text: Few people outside this room will feel this dilemma as directly as the engineers, computer scientists and materials scientists seated here right now. It is you who will ultimately shape the next battery, algorithm or safety protocol.

title.en: Learn the System, Not Just the Part
title.zh: 學整個系統，不只是零件

A2.text: Learn about the whole system, not just one small part. Ask who gets the new smart tools first, and who has to wait longer. Then go and build something useful yourself.

B1.text: Learn to see the whole complicated system, not only one small technical component. Keep asking who gets these smart new tools first, and who is left waiting behind them.

B2.text: Learn to see the whole system rather than any single isolated component. Keep interrogating who actually gains access to these new tools first, and who is left waiting behind everyone else.

title.en: Let's Build It Clean, Smart and Fair
title.zh: 一起蓋出乾淨、聰明又公平的電網

A2.text: We want more than a clean grid. We also want it smart and fair for everyone. Every time you flip a switch, you are now part of building something bigger.

B1.text: Let's build a grid that is not only clean but also genuinely reliable and fair for everyone. Every switch you flip belongs to a system you can now help shape.

B2.text: A truly modern grid must be more than simply clean, since it also needs to be genuinely intelligent, resilient and equitable for everyone involved. The switch flipped in this very room belongs to a system you can now help design.
